UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Case No. 1:26-cv-02331
V.
KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED
CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,
Defendants.
MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO
RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 103
ECF NO. 108 APPLIED A DISCOVERY-POSTPONEMENT RATIONALE TO
JUDICIAL SCHEDULING RELIEF
ECF No. 108 denied judicial scheduling relief because the District Judge had chosen to
postpone discovery. Plaintiff seeks reconsideration of that rationale as applied to the initial-
conference alternative.
ECF No. 108 states its ground in one sentence: "Here, the record reflects that the District
Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions
to dismiss." ECF No. 108 at 2. On that ground, it denied Plaintiff's Motion for Entry of a
Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103) without
prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2.
1

ECF No. 103 requested a scheduling order. ECF No. 103 1| 9, at 3. It separately requested
that, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, the Court
determine whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining
case-management steps. ECF No. 103 9 10, at 3. This Memorandum refers to that second request
as the initial-conference alternative. ECF No. 108 identified it. ECF No. 108 at 1. It denied the
initial-conference request through the same discovery-postponement rationale applied to the
scheduling order. It did not separately explain that application.
The ground for reconsideration is clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson v. Boston
Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Plaintiff presents no new evidence. Plaintiff relies
on no change in law. Plaintiff contends that a rationale directed to the commencement of discovery
was applied to withhold judicial consultation without addressing whether that consultation could
proceed while discovery remained deferred. The resulting postponement has a stated end event. It
has no stated scope and no stated next step.
Plaintiff requests that the Court modify the disposition and set a Rule 16(b) scheduling
conference, with preparatory steps on fixed dates. If the Court determines that the complete
scheduling order should still await the dismissal rulings, Plaintiff requests the initial conference
and the establishment of the remaining case-management steps. In the alternative, Plaintiff
requests that the Court identify the basis and scope of the continued postponement and establish
the step that follows the dismissal rulings. Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B implement
those requests. This Motion does not seek reconsideration of the denial of ECF No. 105.
2

II.
THE RECORD ESTABLISHES THE REQUESTS, THE DISPOSITION, AND
THE ORDINARY SCHEDULING DATE

B.
The ordinary scheduling date was October 13, 2026.
Rule 16(b)(1) applies "[e]xcept in categories of actions exempted by local rule." Fed. R.
Civ. P. 16(b)(1). Local Civil Rule 16(A) exempts "[p]roceedings upon a defendant's default and
matters involving habeas corpus petitions, other pro se prisoner petitions, bankruptcy proceedings,
condemnation cases, forfeitures, and reviews from administrative agencies." Local Civil Rule
16(A). This action is a civil action by a non-prisoner asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2)
and Virginia law. ECF No. 5. It is in none of those categories. Local Civil Rule 16(B) therefore
applies. It directs the Court to schedule an initial pretrial conference "as promptly as possible after
3

a complaint or notice of removal has been filed." Local Civil Rule 16(B). It permits the Court to
enter a scheduling order in addition to, or in lieu of, that conference. It sets the outer time at "not
later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after service of the complaint."
Local Civil Rule 16(B).
Rule 16(b)(2) sets the same outer time and states the exception: "The judge must issue the
scheduling order as soon as practicable, but unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge
must issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint
or 60 days after any defendant has appeared." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Rule 6(a) governs the
computation of "any time period specified in these rules." Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a).

4

Plaintiff does not contend that the lapse affected the Court's jurisdiction, the validity of
any later order, or the Court's authority to find good cause after October 13, 2026. Plaintiff does
not contend that the lapse authorized discovery. ECF No. 103 9 7, at 2. From October 13, 2026
forward, Rule 16(b)(2) permits delay on one condition: that "the judge finds good cause for delay."
Fed. R. CiV. P. 16(b)(2).
C.
The requested and denied relief.
ECF No. 103 moved under Rule 16(b)(1)-(3) and Local Civil Rule 16(B). Its scope section
stated that it sought initial case management and did not seek enforcement of Plaintiff's Rule 26(f)
proposals, authorization of particular discovery, sanctions, or reconsideration of any prior order.
ECF No. 103, Part II, at 3. It did not seek immediate interrogatory responses, document production,
or depositions.
Its relief section requested three things. First, a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference within
21 days, or entry of the scheduling order on a sufficient Rule 26(f) report without a conference,
with the preparatory intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule
26(A)(1). ECF No. 103 99, at 3. Second, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition
of a pending matter, a determination whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now
to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 9 10, at 3. Third, if either step
was postponed, a statement of the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on
which scheduling would next be addressed. ECF No. 103 9 11, at 4. The third request was not
consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 9 12, at 4. The supporting memorandum set out the Rule
16(b)(2) computation and the two routes to a scheduling order under Rule 16(b)(1). ECF No. 104
at 3-5.
ECF No. 108 addressed ECF Nos. 103 and 105 together. It listed the relief requested,
including "an initial pretrial conference." ECF No. 108 at 1. It stated that Plaintiff "has not
5

established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks." ECF No. 108 at 1. It noted the three pending
motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 1. It quoted a decision of the District of Maryland: "Given that
Rule 16 Scheduling Orders initiate discovery obligations, it is standard for courts to wait until any
preliminary motions such as motions to dismiss or to remand are resolved to avoid expensive or
otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims." ECF No. 108 at 1-2 (quoting
Gurri Rubio v. Mullin, No. 25-CV-2756-ABA, 2026 WL 1194557, at *3 (D. Md. May 1, 2026),
appeal dismissed, No. 26-1563 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (per curiam) (unpublished)). It then stated
that "the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery
until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss," and denied both motions without prejudice.
ECF No. 108 at 2.
ECF No. 108 denied the initial-conference request. It did not leave that request undecided.
It applied one rationale to each requested step. It identified the event on which the postponement
ends: resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. It did not state the scope of the postponement
or the step that follows that event.
Ill.
RECONSIDERATION
REQUIRES
MORE THAN
PREFERRED
SCHEDULING APPROACH
Rule 54(b) provides that an order "that adjudicates fewer than all the claims or the rights
and liabilities of fewer than all the parties does not end the action as to any of the claims or parties
and may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all
the parties' rights and liabilities." Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). ECF No. 108 denied case-management
requests without prejudice. It adjudicated no claim. It is an interlocutory order within Rule 54(b).
The Fourth Circuit recognizes the authority Rule 54(b) describes. "[A] district court retains
the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary
judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted." Am. Canoe Ass'n v.
6

Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514-15 (4th Cir. 2003). Motions to reconsider interlocutory
orders "are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final
judgment." Id. at 514.
That authority has limits. A court may revise an interlocutory order in three circumstances:
substantially different evidence produced later in the case; a change in the applicable law; or clear
error causing manifest injustice. Carlson, 856 F.3d at 325 (citing Am. Canoe, 326 F.3d at 515).
Carlson affirmed the denial of reconsideration where the movant relied on deposition testimony
that had been available when the original motion was decided. Id. at 325-26. U.S. Tobacco Coop.
Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256-58 (4th Cir. 2018), applied that framework
and emphasized that Rule 54(b) does not supply an unrestricted opportunity to decide the same
matter differently.
Plaintiff invokes the third circumstance. Plaintiff presents no new evidence. Plaintiff relies
on no change in law. The application Plaintiff challenges concerns requests already presented in
ECF No. 103. The specific attribution to the District Judge appears in ECF No. 108. This Motion
addresses that attribution and its application to the relief previously requested. The attribution's
first appearance in ECF No. 108 does not create a different reconsideration standard. It identifies
what this Motion is about.
Carlson and U.S. Tobacco each addressed revision of a ruling entered by a different judge.
ECF No. 108 was entered by the judicial officer now asked to reconsider it. That circumstance
removes one concern those decisions address. It does not remove the limits they state.
The relief requested is within the Magistrate Judge's authority. Rule 16(b)(1) directs that
"the district judgeor a magistrate judge when authorized by local rule—must issue a scheduling
7

order." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1). Local Civil Rule 26(A)(2) authorizes a magistrate judge to conduct
the scheduling conference and to issue the scheduling order. Local Civil Rule 26(A)(2).
IV. THE STATED RATIONALE SHOULD BE RECONSIDERED AS APPLIED TO
THE INITIAL-CONFERENCE ALTERNATIVE
A. _
Scheduling can proceed while discovery remains regulated.
Three propositions describe the relationship between judicial scheduling and discovery.
Plaintiff relies on all three.
First, judicial consultation at a scheduling conference is not itself document production,
deposition testimony, or an interrogatory response. Rule 16(b)(1)(B) describes the conference as
"consulting with the parties' attorneys and any unrepresented parties at a scheduling conference."
Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1)(B). Rule 16(a) states the purposes a pretrial conference serves, including
"establishing early and continuing control so that the case will not be protracted because of lack
of management" and "discouraging wasteful pretrial activities." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(a)(2) (3).
Second, preparatory steps can affect disclosure and discovery timing. Rule 26(f)(1)
requires the parties to confer "at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a
scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b)," except "when the court orders otherwise." Fed. R. Civ.
P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(a)(1)(C) sets initial disclosures "at or within 14 days after the parties' Rule
26(f) conference unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)
(1)(C). Rule 26(d)(1) restricts discovery before the parties' conference, subject to exceptions that
include a court order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). It does not provide that discovery proceeds after
the conference regardless of court orders. Setting a scheduling conference calls for a parties'
conference. The parties' conference carries timing consequences for disclosures and discovery
unless the Court orders otherwise. Plaintiff does not contend otherwise.
8

Third, the Court can address those consequences expressly while deciding whether judicial
scheduling should proceed. The scheduling order "may" "modify the timing of disclosures under
Rules 26(a) and 26(e)(1)" and "modify the extent of discovery." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(B)(i)-
(ii). At any pretrial conference the Court "may consider and take appropriate action on"
"controlling and scheduling discovery, including orders affecting disclosures and discovery under
Rule 26 and Rules 29 through 37." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(c)(2)(F). Local Civil Rule 16(B) permits the
Court to proceed by scheduling order in addition to, or in lieu of, the initial conference. A court
that intends to defer discovery until the dismissal rulings can state that in the order that follows the
conference, or in a direction entered before it.
A complete scheduling order and an interim case-management direction are different
things. The scheduling order "must limit the time to join other parties, amend the pleadings,
complete discovery, and file motions." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(A). An interim direction that
establishes sequencing and the next step is not a scheduling order unless it contains those limits.
Plaintiff requests the complete order where it can be entered. Where it cannot, Plaintiff requests
the interim direction. A decision to postpone discovery bears on the first. It bears less directly on
the second. ECF No. 108 applied it to both without distinguishing them.
B.
The existing reasons may constitute an implicit good-cause determination.
ECF No. 108 contains no express finding under Rule 16(b)(2). It notes the three pending
motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 1. It quotes the practice of awaiting their resolution to avoid
burdensome discovery. ECF No. 108 at 1-2. It attributes a discovery-postponement decision to the
District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2. Those reasons may be read as an implicit determination that
good cause exists to delay the scheduling order. Plaintiff addresses that reading directly rather than
assume that no determination was made.
9

Plaintiff does not contend that the absence of the words "good cause" is itself error. Rule
52(a)(3) provides that a court "is not required to state findings or conclusions when ruling on a
motion under Rule 12 or 56 or, unless these rules provide otherwise, on any other motion." Fed.
R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). Plaintiff does not contend that each requested step requires its own written
finding. Rule 16(b)(2) governs the time to issue the scheduling order. It sets no separate deadline
for a preliminary conference. Local Civil Rule 16(B) directs the Court to schedule the initial
conference "as promptly as possible" and permits the Court to proceed by order instead.
The question is the reach of the stated reasons. Read as a good-cause determination, those
reasons address discovery burden and the complete schedule. Plaintiff acknowledges four points.
Pending dismissal motions may supply good cause for delaying a complete schedule. Preparing
for a conference consumes the parties' resources. ECF No. 108 identified resolution of the
dismissal motions as the event on which the postponement ends. ECF No. 108 denied the motions
without prejudice.
The stated reasons do not address the initial conference separately. They do not state
whether the determination extends to judicial consultation held while discovery remains deferred,
or why. Plaintiff requests that statement because it would identify the basis and the scope of the
postponement. Plaintiff does not request it on the theory that its omission alone invalidates ECF
No. 108.
ECF No. 108 stated that Plaintiff "has not established that he is entitled to the relief he
seeks." ECF No. 108 at 1. Plaintiff bears the burden on this Motion. Rule 16(b)(2) nonetheless
assigns the scheduling order to the judge: "the judge must issue" it "unless the judge finds good
cause for delay." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Ordinary scheduling is a judicial responsibility. It does
not depend on a party's motion. The question Plaintiff presents is not whether Plaintiff proved
10

entitlement to a particular timetable. It is whether the reasons stated for delay reach the initial-
conference alternative.
C.
The initial conference is the narrower alternative.
ECF No. 103 9| 10, at 3, requested the initial conference as a separate step if the complete
scheduling order should await a pending matter. ECF No. 104 at 4-5 explained the request.
Plaintiff does not assert an unconditional right to that conference. Plaintiff asks the Court to decide
the request under the provisions that govern it.
The conference would accomplish four things. It would identify what prevents completion
of the schedule. It would establish the sequence of the steps that remain. It would establish the step
that follows the dismissal rulings, including after a ruling on fewer than all three motions and after
any ruling that grants leave to amend. It would address preservation under Rule 16(b)(3)(B)(iii)
and the matters Rule 16(c)(2) identifies, to the extent the Court elects to take them up. None of
those steps requires immediate merits discovery. The Court would retain control of every later
step. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b) (4), 16(c)(2)(F).
The strongest reading of ECF No. 108 is not that scheduling and discovery are the same
thing. It is that postponing the linked case-management process avoids work that the dismissal
rulings may make unnecessary. ECF No. 108 may be read to rest on that reading. Plaintiff's
response is narrower than a claim of right. The initial conference could establish sequencing and
the post-disposition procedure without requiring immediate merits discovery. The conference
requires preparation and attendance. If the action remains pending after the dismissal rulings, the
Court will require that work then. If the rulings end the action, the work will have been
unnecessary. That is the cost the practice quoted in ECF No. 108 addresses. It is a cost of
preparation. It is not a cost of discovery. Plaintiff does not contend that the conference is costless.
11

Plaintiff does not contend that its usefulness alone establishes entitlement. Plaintiff asks the Court
to reconsider whether a rationale directed to discovery supports withholding that alternative too.
D.
The source and scope of the attributed decision should be identified.
ECF No. 108 states that "the record reflects" the District Judge's decision. ECF No. 108 at
2. It does not cite the part of the record on which it relies. The District Judge's entries in this action
are listed below.
Entry
ECF No. 12
ECF No. 25
ECF No. 48
ECF No. 50
ECF No. 70
Subject
Denied ECF No. 6 (partial summary
judgment) without prejudice to renewal, as
premature.
Notice advising Plaintiff of the time to
respond to ECF No. 21.
Notice advising Plaintiff of the time to
respond to ECF No. 45.
Directed that ECF No. 10 be decided on the
papers.
Granted leave to file a sur-reply and deemed
it filed.
None of those entries addresses the Rule 16(b) schedule. None expressly postpones it. The
one order that addresses discovery timing is ECF No. 84. Magistrate Judge Davis entered it. It
stated that "discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and
currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case." ECF No. 84 at 1-2. Plaintiff's objections to
ECF No. 84 are pending. ECF Nos. 89, 90. This Motion does not revisit ECF No. 84.
Local Civil Rule 72 permits a magistrate judge to act on the instructions of a district judge.
Local Civil Rule 72. The rule lists that method apart from "an order entered in the action," so an
instruction given that way need not appear on the docket. The local rule establishes the method. It
does not establish that an instruction exists in this action, what it says, or how far it extends.
Three possibilities account for the attribution. First, an instruction of the District Judge
governing discovery only. Second, an instruction also governing scheduling, or reserving
12

scheduling to the District Judge. Third, a case-management determination by the Magistrate Judge
based on the procedural posture of three pending dismissal motions and no scheduling order. Those
possibilities can coexist. The absence of a scheduling order alone does not identify the source or
terms of the attributed decision.
Plaintiff's request is limited. Plaintiff requests identification of any operative order or
instruction to the extent necessary to determine the scheduling obligations in this action and the
scope of the authority referred. Plaintiff does not request internal communications or an account
of judicial deliberation. Plaintiff does not ask the Magistrate Judge to depart from any instruction
of the District Judge. If an instruction governs discovery only, Plaintiff requests the scheduling
determination under Rule 16(b) and Local Civil Rule 16(B). If an instruction also governs
scheduling, Plaintiff requests its operative terms as applied to the scheduling order and to the initial
conference. If an instruction reserves scheduling to the District Judge, Plaintiff requests that the
Order say so, so that the request can be directed accordingly. If the determination is the Magistrate
Judge's own, Plaintiff requests that it be made as to each requested step.
E.
The quotation in ECF No. 108 is addressed as it appears there.
ECF No. 108 quotes Gurri Rubio v. Mullin for the proposition that 'it is standard for courts
to wait until any preliminary motions such as motions to dismiss or to remand are resolved to avoid
expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims." ECF No. 108 at 1
-2. Plaintiff addresses the quotation as it appears in ECF No. 108. Plaintiff does not characterize
that decision beyond its quoted words.
The quotation states a practice and its reason. The reason is avoidance of expensive or
burdensome discovery while a dismissal motion is pending. Plaintiff does not dispute the practice
as a general matter. The quotation does not address whether a court following the practice may
also consult the parties about sequencing before discovery begins. That is the question ECF No.
13

103 9| 10 presented. The quotation's reference to "potentially frivolous claims" describes the
general concern the practice addresses. ECF No. 108 made no finding about Plaintiff's claims, and
Plaintiff reads it as making none.
V.
THE REQUESTED CORRECTION ADDRESSES THE SCHEDULING
CONSEQUENCE
A.
The consequence on the record.
Plaintiff does not contend that delay alone is manifest injustice. Plaintiff does not contend
that an adverse ruling is. Plaintiff does not contend that the Court has stopped managing the action
by giving priority to the dismissal motions. The consequence Plaintiff identifies is procedural, and
the record states it.
The action has three pending dismissal motions, no scheduling order, and no initial
conference. ECF No. 108 applied a discovery rationale to every form of scheduling relief
requested, including the one form that consists of judicial consultation rather than discovery. The
resulting postponement ends on resolution of the dismissal motions. Its scope is not stated. The
parties cannot determine from ECF No. 108 whether the obligations tied to a scheduling
conference are suspended, whether an initial conference is foreclosed until the rulings issue, or
what step follows the rulings.
ECF No. 84 supplies context. It denied Plaintiff's earlier requests because "discovery has
not officially begun in this case" and "currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case." ECF
No. 84 at 1-2. ECF No. 103 then requested the scheduling process itself. ECF No. 108 denied that
request on a discovery rationale. The record now contains two denials that rest on the absence of
the process ECF No. 103 asked the Court to begin. Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84
requires scheduling now. Plaintiff cites it for the consequence of leaving the scheduling process
undefined.
14

The injustice Plaintiff identifies is this: a rationale addressed to discovery was applied to
withhold judicial consultation without a determination that the consultation itself should be
deferred, and the parties were left without a stated scope for the postponement and without a stated
next step. The correction requested is narrow. It asks the Court to decide the initial-conference
alternative under the provisions that govern it and to state the scope of any postponement that
remains.
B.
The initial conference matters despite the ability to renew.
ECF No. 108 denied the motions without prejudice. Renewal after the dismissal rulings is
available. Renewal would present the same request by the same procedure: a motion, briefing, and
a ruling. The initial conference would make that step unnecessary. The Court could establish at the
conference what follows the rulings, including the procedure if the rulings issue on different dates
or grant leave to amend. Rule 16(a)(2) identifies "establishing early and continuing control so that
the case will not be protracted because of lack of management" as a purpose of the conference.
Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(a)(2). A conference held before the rulings establishes the next step in advance.
A motion filed after the rulings asks for it again.
The overlap with ECF No. 105 is accounted for.
ECF No. 103 9 9(c), at 3, requested that the Court shorten the preparatory intervals so that
the parties confer before the Court's conference and file a written report before it. ECF No. 105
requested an order directing the parties to complete their Rule 26(f) conference and submit a
discovery plan. The two motions are distinct. The procedural events they concern overlap. A court-
set scheduling conference calls for a parties' conference under Rule 26(f)(1). That parties'
conference is the event ECF No. 105 addressed.
Proposed Order A accounts for that overlap in three ways. It acts on ECF No. 103. It does
not reconsider the denial of ECF No. 105. It provides that a qualifying parties' conference and
15

report completed before its entry satisfy its preparatory direction, so that no party repeats a
conference or report already completed. Plaintiff does not claim that Proposed Order A has no
effect on the planning process ECF No. 105 addressed. The preparatory direction it contains
follows from Rule 26(f)(1) once the Court sets its conference.
D.
The proposed orders.
Proposed Order A modifies ECF No. 108 only as to ECF No. 103. It sets a scheduling
conference under Rule 16(b)(1)(B) within 21 days after entry, unless a sufficient Rule 26(f) report
permits earlier entry of the scheduling order. It directs the parties' conference and written report
on calendar dates the Court fixes, each after entry, with the intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)
(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1). The report states agreed proposals and each party's
separately attributed position on any matter not agreed, including any position that disclosures or
discovery should await the dismissal rulings.
Proposed Order A creates no stay and extends none. Except as it expressly states, it leaves
the timing of initial disclosures and of discovery to the Federal Rules, the Local Civil Rules, and
the operative orders of the Court. It provides that any additional restriction pending the scheduling
conference must be imposed by an express order identifying its scope and the date or event on
which it ends. Plaintiff does not request a restriction pending the conference. ECF No. 103 9 7, at
2, stated that expiration of the scheduling deadline did not itself authorize discovery. That
statement was not consent to a stay.
After the conference, Proposed Order A provides for one of two things: a scheduling order
under Rule 16(b)(3), or an interim case-management order that identifies the step that remains
before the complete order can be entered, the basis for deferring completion, the case-management
directions established at the conference, and the date or event on which the complete order will be
16

addressed. The interim order is not a scheduling order unless it contains the limits Rule 16(b)(3)
(A) requires.
Proposed Order B applies if the Court continues to postpone both the scheduling order and
the initial conference. It supplies no finding. It provides for the Court to identify any operative
direction of the District Judge being implemented, its application to the scheduling order and to
the initial conference, and the Court's own basis for continuing the postponement. It identifies the
postponed steps separately. It provides that, within 14 days after disposition of the last pending
motion to dismiss, if the action remains pending, the Court will establish the next scheduling step
by entering a scheduling order on a sufficient report, setting a scheduling conference, or directing
a procedure that accounts for any leave to amend. It permits that step earlier where an individual
disposition allows it. No further motion is required. The 14-day period is a requested term.
Plaintiff's request for Proposed Order B is not consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 9| 12, at 4.
17

VI.
CONCLUSION
Plaintiff requests that the Court: (1) reconsider ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No.
103, and modify that disposition; (2) enter Proposed Order A, setting the scheduling conference
and directing the preparatory steps on fixed dates while leaving the timing of disclosures and
discovery to the Court's determination; (3) if the Court determines that the complete scheduling
order should await the dismissal rulings, hold the initial conference and establish the remaining
case-management steps; and (4) in the alternative, enter Proposed Order B, identifying the basis
and scope of the continued postponement and establishing the step that follows the dismissal
rulings. The disposition of ECF No. 105 in ECF No. 108 is outside this Motion and unchanged by
the relief requested.
Date: November 1, 2026
